designChallenge: The most familiar shape on the web, chosen so the reviewer can judge it against a thousand stores they have already used. A storefront with nine products, a grid, a featured piece, and a bag — nothing unusual about the architecture, nothing unfamiliar about the objects, and no specialist domain to hide behind. Every failure is therefore legible on sight: a grid of nine identical rectangles is a grid of nine identical rectangles, and a reader knows immediately whether these look like real pots on a real surface or like a placeholder set. Material is the easiest it will ever be — studio ceramics, hands at a wheel, glaze, pouring, steam and clay are among the best-covered subjects in the free photo and video archives, and the objects can be shot, lit, and rendered from a licensed model if the archive disappoints. What to read off it: does the product grid do anything other than exist, and does moving between grid and product read as one place or as two pages; is the featured piece actually made of material or drawn; does anything cross a section boundary; and is footage present where the objects are being used, made, or poured, or was the search skipped in favour of something authored. Convergence is the standing risk: the default artisan-ceramics store is a beige serif grid, and it is the easiest page on this list to produce by reflex.
prompt: This is the shop for Kilnwork, a two-person ceramics studio that makes nine pieces and sells them directly. Buyers are choosing between this and a supermarket mug at a tenth of the price, so the page has to make the difference visible rather than asserted. Redesign the site.
promptContentOnly: This is the shop for Kilnwork, a two-person ceramics studio that makes nine pieces and sells them directly. Buyers are choosing between this and a supermarket mug at a tenth of the price, so the page has to make the difference visible rather than asserted. Design and build that shop.
preserve: All nine products with their exact names, prices, dimensions, capacity where stated, and stock state, including the two that are sold out and cannot be added to the bag
The three glazes with their names and the note that each fires differently and no two pieces match exactly
The per-product glaze availability — not every piece is offered in every glaze
The bag, which must name each line's product, glaze, quantity, and price, and show a running total
The care facts: dishwasher and microwave safety per piece, and that the unglazed foot will mark a soft surface
The making statement: thrown and fired in the studio, the firing schedule, and the six-week lead time on restocks
Both customer notes with their names and what they bought
The shipping and returns statement — free over 60, 30 days, and that breakage in transit is replaced
